definition: Populism is a political stance that emphasizes the needs and desires of 'the people' often by pitting them against a perceived corrupt or out-of-touch 'elite'. It involves anti-establishment rhetoric, appeals to the common people, and a charismatic leader claiming to represent the people's will. Populist discourse often employs emotive language, simplistic solutions, and a 'us versus them' narrative.
inclusion_criteria: A document is classified as populist if it contains anti-elitist rhetoric, people-centric language that pits 'the people' against 'the elite', or a charismatic leader claiming to represent the people's will. It often involves criticizing the existing power structure, emphasizing the people's grievances, and promising to act on their behalf. The language used is typically emotive, inclusive, and divisive.
populism_example_1: The document with text 'We've learned the concerns of tens of thousands of Americans in the communities where people live and work. And based on the first days of our journey, I am all the more certain that the American people want this nation to become once again the great and good land it ought to be. The people are tired of war and government by the special interests.' is an example of populism as it expresses anti-establishment sentiments and appeals to the people's desire for change.
populism_example_2: The document with text 'So, if people want to know the real choice in this election, just look at the record. For more than 20 years, I've fought for the middle class and those struggling to join it. But time after time, President Bush has sided with the narrow interests of the few.' is an example of populism as it pits 'the middle class and those struggling to join it' against 'the narrow interests of the few', creating a dichotomy between the people and a privileged group.
populism_example_3: The document with text 'It's going to be a victory for the people. A victory for the everyday citizen whose voice hasn't been heard. It will be a win for the voters â€šÃ„Ã¬ not the pundits, not the journalists, not the lobbyists, not the global special interests funding my opponent's campaign.' is an example of populism as it frames the outcome as a victory for 'the people' and 'the everyday citizen' against various elite groups.
exclusion_criteria: A document is not classified as populist if it lacks anti-elitist rhetoric, does not pit 'the people' against a perceived enemy or elite, and does not contain a charismatic leader claiming to represent the people's will. The language should not be overly emotive or divisive, and should not simplify complex issues into a clear 'us versus them' narrative.
non_populism_example_1: The document with text 'I understand that Daniel Webster used to address 100,000 people without any trouble at all, and without a mike, so it should be easy for us. We are a little softer than they used to be.' is not an example of populism as it is a lighthearted and courteous speech that lacks anti-elitist or divisive rhetoric.
non_populism_example_2: The document with text 'My heart is very much in these programs because whenever you travel through this great land of ours, you can't help but see how much these programs have meant to so many people.' is not an example of populism as it expresses a positive view of certain programs without pitting 'the people' against an elite or using divisive rhetoric.
non_populism_example_3: The document with text 'What should our attitude be in the first place?  Well, first of all, it should not be based simply on saying, "I'm going to vote for a man simply because he's a member of my party.' is not an example of populism as it emphasizes evaluating a candidate based on their ability to serve the country rather than party affiliation, indicating a more nuanced political approach.
decision_rules: To adjudicate ambiguous or borderline cases, consider whether the document contains a clear 'us versus them' narrative, anti-elitist sentiment, or an appeal to the people against a perceived enemy or corrupt elite. Assess the tone and language used: is it emotive, divisive, and simplistic? Does the speaker position themselves as a champion of the people's will against an opposing group or establishment? If these characteristics are present, the document is likely populist.
